Wells Fargo Taps Kraken Parent Payward in Push for Deeper Crypto Liquidity

Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, is in talks to become a crypto liquidity provider to Wells Fargo (NYSE: $WFC), according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to CoinDesk.

Under the potential arrangement, Wyoming-based Payward would supply liquidity for digital asset trading, the people said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the discussions are private. Talks remain ongoing and may not result in a deal. Both companies declined to comment.

Crypto exchanges often act as a bridge to digital asset liquidity for banks and institutional investors, providing access to trading venues and helping execute orders. Coinbase Prime, for instance, aggregates liquidity across multiple markets, while Kraken offers banks technology to build crypto trading into their own platforms without constructing the infrastructure themselves.

The discussions add to a pattern of major banks turning to established crypto companies as commercial partners rather than competitors, a shift regulatory changes under the Trump administration have helped accelerate. The GENIUS Act, signed into law in July 2025, created a federal framework for payment stablecoins, giving banks clearer rules for connecting crypto markets to the traditional financial system, a contrast to the period when crypto firms struggled to secure basic banking services.

Anchorage Digital CEO Nathan McCauley told the Senate Banking Committee in February 2025 that more than 40 banks had rejected the company's requests for accounts despite its federal bank charter.

Wells Fargo (NYSE: $WFC) already offers spot Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) ETFs to eligible wealth clients and has backed crypto compliance firm Elliptic and trading technology provider Talos. The bank has also outlined plans for blockchain-based deposits and joined a consortium developing a dollar stablecoin.

Earlier this year, Wells Fargo bolstered its digital assets team by hiring Mark Gracia, a former banker at Citi (NYSE: $C). The bank separately served as Nasdaq's exclusive capital markets adviser on the exchange operator's $100 million investment in Payward announced in September, an agreement that also expanded the two companies' work on tokenized equities and market surveillance.

Investing.com -- Citi Research upgraded elevator maker Kone to "buy" from "neutral" with a €63 price target, saying the shares' fall since February means they price in only a very low probability of its proposed Thyssenkrupp Elevator acquisition.

Before you buy NVIDIA: our AI model's stock picks are beating the market by 120%+. See the list now »

The target was cut from €65 because Citi lowered its long-term growth assumption to 3.0% from 3.5% and raised its discount rate to 7.8% to reflect higher bond yields.

Kone shares closed at €51.72 on Oct. 6. Citi expects a 21.8% share price return and a 25.6% total return including dividends.

Citi values Kone at about €55 a share if the deal falls through, which includes an assumed €1.5 billion break fee.

That is broadly in line with the current price. If the deal goes ahead, it values the combined company at about €68 a share. Its target assumes a 60% chance of the deal completing. Citi called the upside from the deal "essentially a 'free option'" at the current price.

Kone shares trade at about 15.5 times expected 2027 earnings before interest, tax and amortisation, on an enterprise-value basis, against an average of about 18.7 times since 2016. Citi said this reflects fears about rising costs outpacing prices, but it sees only modest downside to consensus 2027 estimates.

Not finding the right stocks? Our AI's list of investor-grade stock picks for October just dropped »

Citi said Kone's estimate of €700 million in annual savings within three years of completion looks credible, even after assumed sales of some businesses. Its own estimates add up to €710 million.

The largest part is service, at €250-300 million. Citi said the combined company would have the world's largest fleet of elevators under maintenance, at 3.2 million units, which could let it grow without hiring technicians as aggressively.

Citi said this could lift the combined service margin above 25%. It also expects double-digit earnings-per-share growth from the deal by the third year and a Kone operating margin of about 17%.

Kone agreed to buy TKE, which is owned by Advent and Cinven, for an enterprise value of €29.4 billion. That includes about €20.2 billion for the shares, paid as €5 billion in cash and about €15.2 billion in new Kone shares. Kone would also refinance about €9.2 billion of net debt.

The deal is under review in major jurisdictions, with the European Union still at the "pre-filing" stage. Kone has said it expects a 12 to 18 month process. Citi said 18 months is more likely a minimum, which would put completion in autumn 2027 or later.

Recently, four major institutions have shared their price predictions for Ethereum (ETH) (CRYPTO:ETH), revealing a wide range of estimates. Citi sets the lowest target at $3,028, while VanEck aims for an ambitious $6,000. Standard Chartered sits in the middle with a target of $4,000, and Bernstein forecasts $5,500. Hitting VanEck's target requires about eight times the gain that Citi's target needs.

As of October 7, 2026, Ether trades at $2,617, having dropped 3% in the last day and approximately 47% from its peak of $4,946. Given these differing projections, which ones seem realistic?

Citi recently updated its 12-month forecast on October 1, increasing its target from $2,240 to $3,028. This means Ether needs to gain around 16% to reach it. Unlike the other forecasts, Citi's target is set for October 2027, allowing Ether about 10 more months than the year-end targets.

Standard Chartered set its year-end target of $4,000 in late May 2026, when Ether was trading below $2,000. To meet this target, Ether needs to increase by roughly 53%. The bank also suggested a longer-term target of $40,000 by the end of 2030, making it unique among the four with a multi-year vision alongside its year-end projection.

UPS shares traded marginally lower in Wednesday's pre-market trade, near $93.08, at the time of writing.

Citi Flags Fuel Prices, Interest Rates

Citi said higher fuel prices and rising interest rates are likely to keep many investors cautious heading into the transportation sector's third-quarter earnings season, according to The Fly.

The brokerage said recent declines in transportation stocks have created a more favorable risk/reward heading into earnings. Citi also adjusted targets on several other transportation stocks, including Union Pacific, J.B. Hunt, FedEx, Werner and TFI International, according to The Fly.

UPS Prepares For Holiday Shipping Season

UPS said it is entering the 2026 holiday shipping season with expanded shipping options, including enhanced shipment tracking and package-protection solutions.

The company said its RFID-powered tracking technology provides more precise, real-time tracking information as packages move through its network. UPS expects to deliver more than 4 billion RFID-enabled packages by the end of 2026.

"We have delivered industry-leading service for eight consecutive peak seasons," Matt Guffey, UPS executive vice president and chief U.S. Domestic Officer, said.

UPS also highlighted greater pickup visibility, simplified returns through UPS and Happy Returns, flexible delivery options and increased automation at facilities in Denver, St. Paul, Syracuse and Portland.

UPS Adds PIN-Based Protected Delivery

UPS introduced Protected Delivery, a service for eligible shipments that requires recipients to provide a PIN to the driver before a package is released.

The company said the service is designed to add an extra layer of security for high-value purchases and other sensitive deliveries during the holiday shipping period.

title: Citi shortens its analyst program to two years as Wall Street fights private equity for young talent
detail:
Citi shortens its analyst program to two years as Wall Street fights private equity for young talent
Citi is taking steps to combat private equity’s poaching of young talent by shortening its analyst program by one year. · Fortune · Michael Nagle—Bloomberg/Getty Images
Sasha Rogelberg
Wed, October 7, 2026 at 2:00 AM CDT 5 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Choosing between becoming a banker or a private equity analyst is akin to the story of the tortoise and the hare. While junior bankers toil with $80,000 salaries in their early years cultivating the fundamentals of finance that will one day bring them success, their counterparts in private equity can make up to $300,000 per year, owning assets and making big decisions. 

The result is a blitz of MBA graduates looking for big names in private equity earlier rather than the less-glitzy promise of a steady career in banking. And as Wall Street continues to swat away threats from private equity to poach young talent, Citi is the latest bank to make changes to retain its junior workforce.

The bank will now transition its analyst program from three years to two, shortening the six-and-a-half-year path to analyst by a year, according to an internal memo—the contents of which were confirmed to Fortune by a Citi spokesperson. The change also applies to junior bankers currently in their third year, who will be promoted Jan. 1 if they meet performance standards.

Talent poaching has long been an issue that every industry has had to contend with, but it seems to be especially prominent in the financial sector, with some banks requiring loyalty oaths from their junior workers promising they haven't accepted roles elsewhere in the first 18 months of their tenure. Taking a jab at banks, private equity firms have begun recruiting fledgling analysts earlier and earlier, pulling college students for "coffee chats" and using "on-cycle" recruiting, or a flurry of interviewing and hiring efforts sometimes two years before candidates officially accept a position.

Wall Street's recurring retention problem

Wall Street has been on high alert about the potential for private equity firms to attract young workers away from banks. While some require the loyalty oaths (which experts warn could backfire through worker resentment of strict policies), others are questioning the young bankers' "character" for accepting such roles. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon called young analysts who take the jobs so early in their career "unethical," arguing even junior bankers who have received limited training are often given access to sensitive information before private equity poaches them. In 2025 JPMorgan told incoming graduates that should they accept a future position elsewhere before completing 18 months as JPMorgan, they would be fired.

David Friedland, Citi's co-head of North America investment banking, expressed a similar view in justifying Citi's decision to condense its career advancement timeline.
